```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5)
has_glmmTMB <- requireNamespace("glmmTMB", quietly = TRUE)
```

This vignette follows Granot, Dubiner & Belmaker (2026). It shows why classic
indices of habitat niche breadth depend on abundance, and how **isoniche**
corrects for it with isodars, using reef fishes from Moorea.

```{r setup}
library(isoniche)
```

## Isodars

Under density-dependent habitat selection, individuals settle where their
expected fitness is highest. As a habitat fills up, its quality declines, so
the next individuals settle in the next-best habitat (the ideal free
distribution; Fretwell & Calver 1969). The densities in two habitats at which
fitness is equal form a line, the *isodar* (Morris 1987):

$$N_2 = a + b N_1 .$$

The intercept $a$ measures a density-independent preference: habitat 2 is
filled with $a$ individuals before habitat 1 receives any. The slope $b$
measures how quickly habitat 2 fills compared with habitat 1 as total
abundance rises. A species without habitat preference has $a = 0$ and
$b = 1$.

Isodars are estimated from replicates (sites, or years at one site) in which
the species' densities in each habitat are known. Because both densities are
measured with error, isodars are fitted by total least squares (major-axis
regression), not by ordinary regression.

## Why abundance-based indices are biased

Whenever an intercept is non-zero, the share of individuals in each habitat
changes with total abundance. A species that is rare spends most of its
individuals in its preferred habitat and looks like a specialist; the same
species, when abundant, spills into other habitats and looks like a
generalist. A classic index, such as 1 - Gini of the habitat proportions,
therefore partly measures abundance:

```{r bias, fig.height = 3.5}
set.seed(2)
sim <- simulate_isodars(slope1 = 1, slope2 = 1, int1 = 8, int2 = 8, noise = 1,
                        n = 60)
classic <- apply(as.matrix(sim[1:3]), 1, function(x) {
  x <- sort(x)
  n <- length(x)
  g <- 2 * sum(seq_len(n) * x) / (n * sum(x)) - (n + 1) / n
  (1 - g - 1 / n) * n / (n - 1)
})
plot(sim$total_abundance, classic, log = "x", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Total abundance at the site", ylab = "Classic niche breadth (1 - Gini)")
```

Every site comes from the same species with the same habitat preferences,
yet niche breadth rises with abundance. Rarefaction (Cayuela et al. 2015)
removes the effect of sampling but not this one, which is part of how the
species uses habitats.

## The data

`moorea_fish` holds counts of 325 reef fish species in three habitats
(barrier reef, fringing reef and outer slope) at 13 sites around Moorea
(BioTIME 2.0; Dornelas et al. 2025). Data are in long format: one row per
species x site x habitat.

```{r data}
head(moorea_fish)
three <- c("Acanthurus nigrofuscus", "Scarus schlegeli", "Siganus argenteus")
fish3 <- moorea_fish[moorea_fish$species %in% three, ]
```

Before fitting, `check_coverage()` shows how many sites sampled each habitat
and whether each habitat would be treated as used, absent or undersampled:

```{r coverage}
cov <- check_coverage(moorea_fish, species = "species", site = "site",
                      habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
table(cov$status)
cov[cov$species %in% three, ]
```

## Pairwise isodars and the n-dimensional isodar

With $H$ habitats there are $H(H-1)/2$ pairwise isodars. They are fitted
separately, each with every site at which both habitats were recorded:

```{r pairwise}
pw <- fit_isodars(fish3, species = "species", site = "site",
                  habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
pw$fit[[1]]
```

The n-dimensional isodar is a *line* through habitat space, not a plane.
Equal fitness in $H$ habitats imposes $H - 1$ equalities, leaving one degree
of freedom: as total abundance changes, densities in all habitats move
together along one line. Its direction says how fast each habitat fills as
abundance rises (the analogue of the slopes), and where it enters each
habitat reflects density-independent preferences (the analogue of the
intercepts). The line is the first principal axis of the site x habitat
densities; `var_explained` measures how well a single line describes them.

```{r line}
ln <- fit_isodars(fish3, species = "species", site = "site",
                  habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance", dim = "ndim")
ln$fit[[3]]
```

## Density-independent and density-dependent niche breadth

The *isodar-adjusted inequality* (IAI) allocates a chosen total abundance
among habitats as the isodars predict and computes 1 - Gini of that
allocation (scaled to 0-1). Two values summarise it:

* **Density-independent (DI) niche breadth**, at the *spillover abundance*
  $T_0$: the smallest total at which every used habitat holds at least one
  individual. It reflects the intercepts.
* **Density-dependent (DD) niche breadth**, as total abundance tends to
  infinity, where only the slopes (the direction of the line) matter.

```{r nb}
nb <- niche_breadth(fish3, species = "species", site = "site",
                    habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance",
                    n_boot = 199, seed = 1)
nb[c("species", "nb_di", "nb_di_lower", "nb_di_upper", "spillover_abundance",
     "nb_dd", "nb_dd_lower", "nb_dd_upper")]
```

Pairwise isodars are combined by weighted least squares; by default each is
weighted by its inverse variance, $1 / (sd^2 (1 + b^2))$, as in the paper
(`weights = "1/var"`). Intervals come from resampling whole sites
(`n_boot`).

Between $T_0$ and infinity, while no two habitats swap rank,
$$NB(T) = NB_{DD} + (NB_{DI} - NB_{DD}) \frac{T_0}{T},$$
so niche breadth is halfway between the two values at $T = 2T_0$. Where the
predicted abundances of two habitats cross, the curve changes course; these
*preference reversals* are reported, as are habitats used at low density and
abandoned at high density:

```{r reversals}
nb$abandoned
nb$reversals[[1]]
```

## Niche breadth curves

`iai_curve()` computes the whole curve, like a rarefaction curve for
niche breadth. In the plot, the filled point is each species' DI value at
its own spillover abundance, the dash on the right its DD value, crosses
mark preference reversals and dotted lines the bootstrap band.

```{r curve, fig.height = 5}
curve <- iai_curve(ln, n_boot = 99, seed = 1)
plot(curve, abundances = 1000, crossings = TRUE)
```

Species can swap rank: whether one is a broader generalist than another
depends on the abundance at which they are compared. The crossings are
returned as a table:

```{r crossings}
attr(curve, "crossings")
```

Plotting against abundance relative to $T_0$ puts all DI values at 1:

```{r curve-relative, fig.height = 5}
plot(curve, x_axis = "relative")
```

## Diagnostics

`niche_breadth()` never stops on a problem species and does not print one
warning per species. Each potential problem is a logical `flag_*` column,
summarised in `flags`:

```{r flags}
all_nb <- niche_breadth(moorea_fish, species = "species", site = "site",
                        habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance",
                        n_boot = 0, seed = 1)
all_nb
sort(colSums(as.data.frame(all_nb[grep("^flag_", names(all_nb))])),
     decreasing = TRUE)
```

Among them, `flag_intercept_noise` marks species whose intercepts do not
differ from those produced by sampling alone (a multinomial null model, as
in section 1.2.3 of the paper): for these species, DI and DD niche breadth
cannot be told apart. Thresholds are set through `diagnostics`, for
example `diagnostics = list(min_sites = 8)`.

## Absent habitats

A habitat in which a species was never recorded, although it was sampled at
several sites where the species was present, is treated as *absent*: it is
fixed at 0, excluded from the isodar fit and counted as 0 in the
inequality, so it lowers niche breadth. With `absent = "auto"` a habitat is
absent if the species was counted there no more than `absent_max_count`
times (default 0) across at least `absent_min_sites` (default 5) such sites;
with fewer sites the zeros may reflect undersampling, and the species is
flagged instead. A species found in a single habitat has niche breadth 0.

Because absent habitats lower niche breadth, species should be compared over
the same set of habitats: the habitats available to them.

## Incomplete sites

Often not every habitat exists, or was sampled, at every site. Pairwise
isodars use every site with both habitats of a pair. For the line,
`ndim_method = "latent"` fits a one-factor model to every site with at least
two habitats, so incomplete sites contribute (this needs **glmmTMB**):

```{r latent, eval = has_glmmTMB}
set.seed(1)
inc <- simulate_isodars(slopes = c(1.5, 1, 0.8), intercepts = c(5, 0, 2),
                        n = 80, p_missing = 0.3)
fit_isodars(inc, hab_cols = c("hab1", "hab2", "hab3", "hab4"), dim = "ndim",
            ndim_method = "latent")
```

When sites are small, nearby sites can be grouped with `group_sites()`
(complete linkage, so every pair of sites in a group lies within the radius).
The radius is not chosen automatically, because choosing it to improve the
results would be circular; `radius_sensitivity()` shows how the number of
units, their completeness and niche breadth change with it.

## Effort and units

Isodars relate *densities*. If sampling effort differs among sites or
habitats (area, transect length, or a unitless relative effort), give it in
an `effort` column: densities are abundance / effort, expressed per
`reference_effort` (by default the median effort). "One individual" at the
spillover abundance means one individual per reference effort, so DI niche
breadth and the spillover abundance depend on this unit, whereas slopes and
DD niche breadth do not. Replicates can be sites or time steps.

## Indices from isodar parameters (Appendix S1)

`pairwise_niche()` summarises the pairwise isodars directly: the mean
intercept and slope, and the inverse root-mean-square deviations of slopes
from 1 and of intercepts from 0. The intercept index is in abundance units,
so it depends on effort.

```{r appendix}
pairwise_niche(pw$fit[[1]], weights = "1/var")
```
